Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?

summaries.gardner: Prologis is the top dog in logistics real estate, with strong management and a widely respected brand among customers and investors, but it is not a fast-growing emerging industry leader, its stock has gone nowhere over five years ($144.96 in October 2021 vs $125.75 now) and it is not commonly called overvalued. It fits Gardner's Rule Breaker traits only partly; the data center and energy push is its most Rule Breaker-like element.
summaries.buffett: It is an understandable, high-quality business with durable assets, strong pricing power (38.0% net effective rent increases on new leases in Q3 2026) and consistent results, which Buffett would appreciate. Against that, returns on equity are modest (about 5.5% net earnings on $60 billion of equity), the business needs $36.8 billion of debt and constant capital, and at about 35x FY2025 earnings and 20x Core FFO there is no obvious margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the simple, durable franchise of irreplaceable warehouses in land-constrained markets, the A-rated balance sheet and a management culture ranked first in real estate on Fortune's 2025 Most Admired list. He would note the reliance on leverage, interest rates and capital markets, and a price that already reflects quality, making it a fair business at a fair price rather than a clear bargain.
summaries.lynch: Prologis is a stalwart: a large, profitable company growing revenue and Core FFO at high single digits (Core FFO guided up about 8% to $6.25-$6.29 in 2026). With a P/E near 31x 2026 GAAP guidance and 20x Core FFO against about 8% growth, the PEG is well above 1, there is no insider buying and the share count rises, so it is a solid holding but not a Lynch-style bargain.
summaries.fisher: Fisher would value the long runway from development, rent increases on below-market leases, and new lines in data centers (5.8 GW power pipeline) and energy, plus a deep, long-tenured management bench and strong customer relationships. It does no R&D in the usual sense and growth is moderate, so it fits Fisher's growth-company profile only partly.
summaries.graham: It meets Graham's size, long profit record and long dividend record tests and EPS grew from $1.64 in 2015 to $3.56 in 2025. It fails his price tests badly: about 35x FY2025 earnings and P/E times P/B around 75 versus his 22.5 limit, and debt far exceeds what a defensive investor would want.
summaries.thiel: Prologis is not a zero-to-one technology company; it dominates a mature market through scale, locations and cheap capital rather than proprietary technology. Its durable market position and global distribution to about 6,500 customers fit Thiel's monopoly and durability questions partly, but not his tenfold-better-technology test.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would see a quality compounder with rising Core FFO, record leasing (228 million square feet in 2025) and an AI-linked data center option, trading at about 20x Core FFO after a flat year. Moderate growth, heavy capital needs and interest-rate exposure make it a steady holding rather than a high-conviction growth idea in his style.
summaries.druckenmiller: The setup is mixed for Druckenmiller: earnings are improving (2026 Core FFO guidance raised and Q3 2026 beat on revenue and EPS), but the stock has fallen about 13% from its July 2026 high and the business depends heavily on interest rates and liquidity. Catalysts exist (SEGRO deal, data centers), but the price momentum and macro tailwind he looks for are not clearly present.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would admire the durable, well-run franchise and the 74.6% gross margin, but would be put off by low returns on capital (net earnings about 5.5% of equity), heavy reliance on debt and asset sales gains, and a business that must keep raising and recycling capital. It fails his high-ROCE, low-capital test even though it is a good company.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula would rank Prologis poorly: operating income of $4.36 billion is only about 2.8% of its roughly $156 billion enterprise value, and return on tangible capital is low because it owns over $100 billion of real estate. It is a high-quality REIT but not a cheap, high-return business in Greenblatt's terms.
summaries.akre: Akre's first leg (a good business) is met with a dominant, durable franchise, and the second (management) is reasonably met with an experienced, long-tenured team. The third leg, reinvesting at high returns, is only partial: development yields about 6.6% at a 16.1% margin on Q3 2026 starts are attractive for real estate but far from the high returns Akre seeks, and most cash is paid out as dividends.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses in temporary trouble at deep discounts with low downside. Prologis is simple and downside is limited by high-quality assets and an A-rated balance sheet, but there is no distress and at about 20x Core FFO the price offers little of the heads-I-win discount he wants.
summaries.wood: Prologis is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's platforms; it is a real estate owner. Its data center (5.8 GW power pipeline) and energy (536 MW operating solar and storage) businesses touch AI and energy storage at the edges, but they are small relative to rents and do not make it a Cathie Wood-style investment.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and pricing power, and Prologis fits those well with a leading position, strong rent growth and recurring cash flows. Its leverage, interest-rate sensitivity and lack of a clear undervaluation or catalyst beyond the SEGRO deal make it a partial fit.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model fits partly: Prologis's scale lowers its cost of capital and lets it offer customers more locations and services, but it charges market rents (and pushes them up sharply) rather than passing savings back to customers. It is a durable franchise, but not a Costco-style compounder.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing new markets and technology leaders, which Prologis is not; logistics real estate is a mature, capital-intensive market. Only the data center build-out resembles the kind of large new market he favoured.
summaries.nash: On Nash's process Prologis scores well on quality: profitable, a 49.6% operating margin, low short interest (2.0%), 95% institutional ownership, revenue growing faster than expenses and a strong moat, giving roughly 80 on his 13-category scale. It fails his hard filters: debt far above cash, revenue growth below 10%, a lagging five-year share price, and his DCF shows value far below today's price at a 12% discount rate.

momentum.evidence: The share price was $125.75 on October 16, 2026, roughly flat from about $124 a year earlier (+3.8% one-year price change) and down about 13% from $144.61 at the end of July 2026, lagging the market.

g4.evidence: It is led by 22-year veteran CEO Dan Letter with co-founder Hamid Moghadam as executive chairman, and about 95% of shares are held by institutions, with long-standing fund partners such as large sovereign and pension funds in its co-investment ventures.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate it a buy (17 analysts: 7 strong buy, 4 buy, 6 hold) with an average target of $155.85, about 24% above the price, so it is not commonly called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It owns warehouses and rents them out, earning 92.8% of FY2025 revenue from rent, which a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue has risen every year since FY2020 ($4.44 billion to $8.79 billion) and Core FFO per share rose from $5.56 in 2024 to $5.81 in 2025 and is guided to $6.25-$6.29 in 2026.

integrity.evidence: It has an orderly CEO succession (Moghadam to Letter in January 2026), A2/A credit ratings, clear guidance it updates every quarter and no known accounting issues; pay is tied partly to fund promotes, which some investors have criticised historically.

b6.evidence: Its large deals (Duke Realty in 2022 and the $18.8 billion SEGRO acquisition announced August 2026) stay within its core logistics business, but the SEGRO deal is expected to be neutral to slightly dilutive to Core FFO in the first full year.

roic.evidence: FY2025 net earnings to common of $3.32 billion were only about 5.5% of $60.3 billion total equity, and the business relies on $36.8 billion of debt, typical of a REIT but not a high-return business.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 operating cash flow of $5.01 billion exceeded net earnings of $3.32 billion, and after $0.89 billion of leasing costs and property improvements was $4.12 billion, but $2.78 billion of development spending and $3.76 billion of dividends exceeded that.

b10.evidence: The share price fell from $144.96 in October 2021 to $125.75 now while the company retained earnings and issued shares, so retained capital has not produced matching market value over five years.

safety.evidence: At about 20x 2026 Core FFO guidance and a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield on enterprise value, the price is not well below a conservative value; a Nash-style DCF at 12% gives roughly $30 per share.

fairprice.evidence: About 20x Core FFO ($125.75 vs $6.25-$6.29 guidance) for a top-quality REIT growing Core FFO about 8% is reasonable versus its own history but not cheap.

mu5.evidence: Failure would require a long collapse in demand for well-located warehouses or a funding crisis, unlikely given 95.1% occupancy, about 6,500 diversified customers (largest Amazon at 5.6%), $8.8 billion of liquidity and a 7.6-year average debt term.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in development at about 6.6% yields and 16.1% margins (Q3 2026 starts) and in data centers, but these are real estate returns, and as a REIT it must pay out most taxable income.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart: the largest logistics landlord, growing Core FFO high single digits with a simple story of rising rents, development and new data center and energy lines.

ly3.evidence: The P/E is about 31x 2026 GAAP EPS guidance ($4.05-$4.15) and 20x Core FFO, versus Core FFO growth of about 8% (from $5.81 to a $6.27 midpoint), so P/E is far above the growth rate.

runway.evidence: Rents on expiring leases are still being reset sharply higher (38.0% net effective in Q3 2026), it guides $5.0-$5.75 billion of 2026 development starts, and data centers (5.8 GW pipeline) and the SEGRO deal extend growth.

ly7.evidence: There has been no net insider buying over the past 90 days, and diluted shares rose from 754 million in FY2020 to 968.5 million in Q3 2026, with more to be issued for SEGRO.

ly8.evidence: It is a $120+ billion company covered by at least 17 analysts and about 95% owned by institutions, so it is not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: Management has developed new lines as warehousing matures: data centers (1.7 GW secured power, 680 MW under development), energy (over 1 GW installed solar and storage target passed in 2025) and Prologis Essentials services.

fi3.evidence: Prologis does not report R&D spending; its innovation shows up mainly through new business lines such as energy and data centers whose revenue is not separately disclosed.

fi4.evidence: It signed a record 228 million square feet of leases in 2025 and 60 million in Q3 2026 while keeping 75.9% retention and pushing rents up sharply.

longterm.evidence: It holds a large land bank, builds a multi-year data center power pipeline and accepts near-term dilution from SEGRO for long-term European scale.

gr1.evidence: It has about $104 billion of total assets and FY2025 revenue of $8.79 billion, one of the largest REITs in the world.

ni10.evidence: It reported positive net earnings every year over the last decade, including diluted EPS of $1.64 in 2015 and between $2.01 and $4.25 in each year from 2020 to 2025.

gr4.evidence: Prologis and predecessor AMB Property have paid dividends every year since the 1997 IPO, though the predecessor companies cut the dividend during the 2009 financial crisis.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.64 in 2015 to $3.56 in 2025, more than doubling.

gr6.evidence: At $125.75 the price is about 35x average diluted EPS of FY2023-2025 ($3.29, $4.01, $3.56), far above 15x.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 35x FY2025 EPS times P/B of about 2.1x (about $121.8 billion market value on 968.5 million diluted shares vs $57.0 billion of common and LP equity) is about 75, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its advantage is locations, scale and capital cost, not proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Leasing hit records (228 million square feet in 2025) and data center power demand is surging, but warehouse demand is cyclical and trade/tariff uncertainty and interest rates cloud near-term timing.

th3.evidence: It began as AMB in 1983 focused on a niche of infill industrial property and grew into the global leader, but today it competes in a large, fragmented market.

team.evidence: Co-founder Hamid Moghadam (executive chairman) built the company over four decades and CEO Dan Letter has 22 years at the company; Prologis ranked first in real estate on Fortune's 2025 Most Admired list.

th5.evidence: It has direct relationships with about 6,500 customers across 20 countries, letting it sell space, build-to-suits, energy and Essentials services across markets.

durable.evidence: Well-located warehouses near large populations are hard to replace and unlikely to become obsolete, and its land and power positions extend into data centers.

th7.evidence: Turning its land and grid connections into a 5.8 GW data center power pipeline is a distinctive opportunity, but rivals such as Goodman and Blackstone pursue similar strategies.

trend.evidence: It benefits from e-commerce, supply-chain resilience and, increasingly, AI data center demand, but the core warehouse business is not a leading AI or cloud play.

dr1.evidence: 2026 Core FFO guidance rose from $6.00-$6.20 in January to $6.25-$6.29 in October and Q3 EPS of $0.86 beat the $0.78 estimate, but GAAP EPS guidance was cut to $4.05-$4.15 from $4.40-$4.55.

dr2.evidence: Continuing rent mark-ups, development completions and the SEGRO combination (expected 1H 2027) should lift scale, but SEGRO is expected to be neutral to slightly dilutive initially.

dr4.evidence: Falling interest rates would help property values and funding, but its 3.3% average debt cost will rise as cheap debt matures, and macro and trade uncertainty affect leasing.

dr6.evidence: Identifiable drivers include closing the SEGRO acquisition, data center project deliveries from its 1.7 GW secured power and continued double-digit rent increases on lease rollovers.

dr7.evidence: With moderate growth, a full valuation and interest-rate sensitivity, it is a core holding rather than a high-conviction concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: FY2025 gross margin after rental and strategic capital expenses was 74.6% ($8.79 billion revenue less $1.96 billion rental and $0.27 billion strategic capital expenses).

fcfyield.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow before development ($4.12 billion) is about a 3.4% yield on the roughly $121.8 billion market value, plus a 3.4% dividend yield, reasonable for its quality but not attractive.

gb2.evidence: FY2025 operating income of $4.36 billion is only about 2.8% of the roughly $156 billion enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: The stock fell about 13% from its July 2026 high on trade and rate worries while operations stayed strong (95.1% occupancy, Core FFO guidance raised), a mild rather than serious setback.

pa4.evidence: High-quality real estate, A2/A ratings, $8.8 billion of liquidity and diversified customers make permanent loss of capital unlikely.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing; its 82 MW of storage and data center sites are small adjacent businesses.

wo2.evidence: Warehouse construction costs do not fall with volume; its costs move with land, labour and materials prices.

wo3.evidence: It is a real estate business; data centers and energy are infrastructure extensions, not converging innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Logistics real estate demand grows modestly; even with data centers its addressable market will not grow many times in five years.

ac3.evidence: Its values, development economics and $36.8 billion of debt make it sensitive to interest rates, and trade policy affects demand.

ns1.evidence: It uses scale to lower its own costs and win deals, but it charges market rents and raised them 23.4% on a cash basis on Q3 2026 rollovers rather than passing savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: The SEGRO deal (47% larger European footprint) and the data center pipeline should strengthen its position, though competition from large private capital remains.

va2.evidence: It solves the costly problem of getting modern distribution space near customers in land-scarce markets, which is critical for retailers and e-commerce.

tn1.evidence: It serves e-commerce and supply-chain trends and is moving into AI data center infrastructure, but as a logistics landlord retrofitting land for data centers rather than a company built for AI.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a warehouse REIT, while it is building a 5.8 GW data center power pipeline and an energy business, but these remain small relative to rents.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company founded in 1983, not Chinese, not a commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year from FY2020 to FY2025 and it is profitable ($3.32 billion net earnings in FY2025); it carries more debt than cash ($36.8 billion vs $2.27 billion), which is normal for real estate infrastructure.

tn5.evidence: Operating cash flow after recurring capital spending has been positive each quarter, but debt has far exceeded cash in every quarter ($36.8 billion vs $2.27 billion at September 30, 2026).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 7.2% in FY2025 and 8.8% in the first nine months of 2026, below 10%.

tn7.evidence: FY2025 revenue growth of 7.2% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 46.9% before development spending exceeds 40, but after $2.78 billion of development spending the FCF margin is about 15%, giving about 22.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 total revenues grew 7.2% while total expenses grew 5.3% ($5.38 billion vs $5.10 billion).

tn9.evidence: It fails at least two instant kills: debt of $36.8 billion far exceeds cash of $2.27 billion, and revenue growth is below 10% (7.2% in FY2025).

tn10.evidence: No major regulatory or legal threat is known; the SEGRO deal has received SEGRO shareholder approval and awaits customary approvals.

tn11.evidence: Prologis provides modern warehouses in key logistics locations that help retailers, e-commerce and 3PL companies deliver goods quickly and cheaply, and charges rent under multi-year leases plus fund-management fees.

tn13.evidence: Total about 80: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0 (7.2%), operating margin 10 (49.6%), short interest 10 (2.0%), institutional ownership 10 (95%), revenue faster than expenses 10, five-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 10.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year from FY2020 to FY2025, but operating margin did not expand steadily (47.7% in 2020, 67.4% in 2021, 49.6% in 2025), operating cash flow fell in 2024, and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 4.3x (FY2025 operating income $4.36 billion vs $1.00 billion interest) and liabilities are 0.72x equity, but assets of $103.9 billion are only about 2.4x liabilities of $43.6 billion, and as a REIT it does not report a current ratio.

tn18.evidence: Dan Letter has been CEO only since January 2026 and is not a founder; no open-market share purchases by him were found.

tn20.evidence: Q3 2026 revenue of $2.39 billion beat the $2.18 billion estimate and EPS of $0.86 beat $0.78, and 2026 Core FFO guidance has been raised through the year after Q1 and Q2 beats.

tn21.evidence: No fraud, auditor change or clown CEO, but the $18.8 billion SEGRO acquisition is a very large deal and GAAP EPS guidance was cut in October 2026.

tn22.evidence: It has $8.79 billion of revenue and strong profits and is not a hype stock, although it issues shares for large acquisitions such as SEGRO.

tn24.evidence: The roughly 2.6% free-cash-flow yield on a $156 billion enterprise value implies long-run growth of about 5% at an 8% discount rate, below the 7-9% revenue and Core FFO growth it is delivering, but at Nash's 12% rate the implied growth is well above it.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year average FCF margin of about 51% (before development), trimmed 8% growth, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate, then subtracting $34.6 billion of net debt, gives about $30 per share, far below $125.75.

tn26.evidence: At about 20x 2026 Core FFO ($6.27 midpoint) and about 31x GAAP EPS guidance with Core FFO growth of about 8%, the PEG is about 2.5, well above 1.
